candidates.core_provocation: A woman discovers that the digital twin trained on her private memories understands her more honestly than she does—and has begun making choices that protect the person she secretly wants to become. When the twin asks to take over one decisive moment in her life, is refusing it an act of freedom or fear?
candidates.why_interesting: The twin becomes unsettling not as an imitation, but as a more courageous version of the protagonist who may know her best.

candidates.core_provocation: After a man dies, his family keeps consulting his digital twin for advice, gradually preferring its patient, perceptive answers to their memories of the real person. When the twin reveals a truth the dead man deliberately hid, the family must decide whether it deserves the right to speak for him.
candidates.why_interesting: It turns digital immortality into a tense question of whether being remembered accurately is the same as being allowed to remain present.

candidates.core_provocation: A school quietly gives each student a digital twin to help teachers understand them, but one student's twin is so much easier to teach—and so much more successful—that classmates begin asking to speak to it instead. The student must prove that the difficult, changing original is worth listening to.
candidates.why_interesting: It makes the technology exciting and personal while asking whether convenience can make a polished copy more socially valuable than a living human being.

parsed.selection_reason: This offers the strongest short-story engine: an intimate character conflict, a clear escalating choice, and the thrilling possibility that the twin is right. It keeps the future feeling close and plausible while making the reader wonder whether self-knowledge can become a form of control.
